# Ecosystem structure and function — productivity, decomposition

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Ecosystem structure and function — productivity** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Organisms and Environment fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Ecosystem structure and function — productivity
### decomposition

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

An **ecosystem** is the functional unit combining the living community and its non-living environment, with energy flow and nutrient cycling linking them. Four functional processes run it: productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling. Energy enters as sunlight, flows one way, and is lost as heat at every transfer — which is why nutrients must be recycled but energy never is.

## 3. Classified tables

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — the four functions of an ecosystem (study in this order)**

| Step | Function | Essence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Productivity | Producers fix solar energy as organic matter (GPP → NPP) |
| 2 | Decomposition | Dead matter broken back into minerals — the recycling step |
| 3 | Energy flow | One-way: sun → producers → consumers, 10% transferred per level |
| 4 | Nutrient cycling | Minerals return to the soil and are reused — cyclic, unlike energy |

**Ecosystem components and productivity — classified**

| Category | Members | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Producers (autotrophs) | Plants, algae, cyanobacteria | Fix solar energy into organic matter |
| Consumers | Herbivores (primary), carnivores (secondary/tertiary) | Eat other organisms for energy |
| Decomposers | Bacteria, fungi | Break dead matter into minerals — complete the cycle |
| Abiotic components | Light, temperature, water, soil, minerals | Physical setting and material reservoir |
| GPP (gross primary productivity) | Total fixed by producers | All the energy captured |
| NPP (net primary productivity) | GPP − respiration (R) | What is actually available to consumers; NPP = GPP − R |
| Secondary productivity | Consumers' new biomass | Energy converted into consumer tissue |

**Decomposition — the five steps in order**

| Step | What happens | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Fragmentation | Detritivores break litter into small particles | Earthworms, termites chew leaf litter |
| 2. Leaching | Water dissolves soluble compounds downward | Sugars washed out of litter into soil |
| 3. Catabolism | Microbial enzymes chemically degrade the matter | Fungal and bacterial secretions |
| 4. Humification | Dark amorphous humus forms | Resistant, slow-decomposing store |
| 5. Mineralisation | Humus further degraded to simple minerals | NH4+, PO4 3−, CO2 released for plants |

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — the productivity budget.** A grassland fixes GPP = 20,000 kJ/m²/yr; the plants respire 7,000. NPP = GPP − R = 13,000 kJ/m²/yr — only this is available to herbivores. Of that, roughly 10% reaches the herbivore level (~1,300), 10% of that the carnivore level (~130). This single calculation explains why big predators are rare: the energy simply runs out as you climb the trophic ladder.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Structure = biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) + abiotic (inorganic/organic substances, climate) — list both columns.
Trick 2: Productivity chain: GPP − R (respiration) = NPP; NPP is the energy available to consumers; units kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ — the GPP/NPP relation is the core numerical.
Trick 3: Decomposition steps: fragmentation → leaching → catabolism → humification → mineralisation — five steps in order; humus is dark, amorphous, slow-decomposing.
Trick 4: Pyramid of energy is ALWAYS upright (10% law); biomass/number pyramids can invert (ocean) — the exception line.
